title: Knowing your price
hook: Agrippinus kept his character though it cost him; each person knows their own price (Discourses 1.2)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prohairesis, the will that not even Zeus can overpower. Your line was what is still yours.

Agrippinus is being tried before the Senate in Rome. A messenger runs to tell him. Agrippinus says: good luck to it. But it's the hour for exercise and a cold bath. Let's go. Later the messenger comes back. You've been condemned. To exile, or to death? Exile. And my property? Not taken. Then let's go out to Aricia and have lunch. Epictetus tells that one in the first discourse. In the second, he tells another story about him, about a question Agrippinus refused even to think about.
screen: `AGRIPPINUS, ON TRIAL.` → `EXILE? THEN LET'S HAVE LUNCH.` → `KNOWING YOUR PRICE.`

segments.voice: The second discourse is titled, roughly, how to keep your own character in everything. The Greek word for character there is prosōpon, the mask and role from the handbook. Epictetus imagines someone asking whether to hold the chamber pot for another man. If he refuses, he'll be beaten and go without food. For a different person, it would be unbearable not only to hold it, but even to let someone else hold it for him. If you ask me, Epictetus says, I'll tell you food is worth more than hunger and a beating is worse than none, so if that's how you measure, go and hold it. But it's beneath me? That, he says, is something you bring to the question, not me. You know what you're worth to yourself, and at what price you sell yourself. People sell themselves at different prices. Then Agrippinus. A man named Florus was weighing whether to take part in one of Nero's spectacles, appearing on stage to please the emperor. He asked Agrippinus, who said: go. Then why won't you? Because, said Agrippinus, I don't even consider the question. Once you start weighing such things, Epictetus says, setting the value of outside things against each other, you're close to those who've forgotten their own character. Agrippinus didn't win the argument about Nero's stage. He never let it become an argument. Knowing your price isn't pride. It's knowing, before the offer arrives, the few things that simply aren't for sale.
screen: `KEEP YOUR CHARACTER IN EVERYTHING.` · `YOU KNOW AT WHAT PRICE YOU SELL YOURSELF.` · `I DON'T EVEN CONSIDER THE QUESTION.` · `SOME THINGS AREN'T FOR SALE.` · then, large: `I KNOW MY PRICE.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself quietly what you wouldn't do, even if it paid well, even if everyone else was doing it: laughing at a cruel joke to fit in, shading the truth for a sale, flattering someone to get ahead. Find one, and picture the moment it's offered. Then picture yourself not even weighing it, just a plain no.
Agrippinus. The man who wouldn't even consider some questions; you know at what price you sell yourself. Today's word.
Your line: I know my price. Some questions never need weighing at all, not even once. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes decide in advance on a few things they will not do for any reward, so that when the offer comes they don't have to deliberate.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.1.28–32 (Agrippinus' trial and lunch at Aricia)

notes: Discourses 1.1.28–32 paraphrased: Agrippinus told he is being tried in the Senate; goes to exercise and bathe; condemned to exile; property not confiscated; 'let us go to Aricia and dine'. Confirm section numbers.

Discourses 1.2 paraphrased: title on preserving one's character (prosōpon) in everything; the chamber-pot example; 'you know how much you are worth to yourself and at what price you sell yourself; men sell themselves at different prices'; Florus considering going down to Nero's spectacles; Agrippinus: 'go down'; 'I do not even consider the question'; whoever stoops to such consideration is near to forgetting his character. Confirm.
1.2 also contains a passage about suicide by hanging as an example of the 'reasonable'; deliberately omitted.
Helvidius Priscus and the purple stripe (also in 1.2) are left for tomorrow.

The chamber-pot holder is glossed as 'an enslaved man asking whether to hold the chamber pot for his master'; the Greek speaks of holding it for another, with beating and loss of food as the stakes, which implies servitude but does not name it. Confirm the gloss is fair.
The hook places Agrippinus' trial 'under Nero'; Paconius Agrippinus was exiled in 66/67 (Tacitus, Annals 16.28-33). Epictetus' account does not name the emperor in 1.1. Confirm.
